text.brief: On July 20, 1982, the nineteen-year-old tennis player Hu Na left her team's hotel in Santa Clara and later sought asylum in the United States.
text.record: She told American officials she feared persecution at home and had resisted pressure to join the Party. The Party demanded her return and warned of harm to relations. The Reagan administration granted her asylum on April 4, 1983 ([Christian Science Monitor, April 8, 1983 (media only)](https://www.csmonitor.com/1983/0408/040870.html); [Christian Science Monitor, April 5, 1983 wire digest (media only)](https://www.csmonitor.com/layout/set/amphtml/1983/0405/040524.html)). Three days later the Party canceled nineteen sports and cultural exchanges planned for the rest of the year.
text.reading: The Party punished a whole program for one woman's choice, which is Stratagem 26, and it priced every future defection in lost access. The pressure ran down a gradient from a single athlete to every American institution that valued the exchanges.
text.gapText: Business Architecture. No one owned the exchanges as a whole, so the Party could cancel them at no cost to itself.
text.fix: Plan exchanges so that a cancellation costs the side that cancels, and state in advance that asylum decisions will not bend to reprisal.
